newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Outlook positive for Hysan - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Outlook positive for Hysan - analysts.

text.p: Hong Kong property investor Hysan Development Co Ltd posted a 10 percent rise in 1996 net profit on Wednesday and although growth was below market consensus, analysts said they were optimistic about the future.

Hysan reported net profit of HK$1.35 billion for calendar 1996, below market forecasts of between HK$1.36 billion and HK$1.41 billion. "Barring unforseen circumstances, the group's performance for 1997 is expected to be satisfactory," it said.
Turnover rose to HK$2.22 billion in 1996 compared with HK$1.96 billion in 1995.
"The figure is disappointing," said Desmond Cheung, an associate director at Vickers Ballas.
Analysts suspected the shortfall might have come from lower rental income growth than the 14 percent they had predicted, or from an overestimate of investment income from securities.
They said about 75-80 percent of the company's profit was from rental income with the remainder generated from investments in securities and properties.

Hysan said its existing office and retail properties were virtually fully let and office rental levels were firm. The company said rents for its luxury residential properties, which were about 97 percent let, had risen.
It said all units of its Melville Park residential project in Singapore were sold and profit generated would be distributed to shareholders as a dividend.

About a third of the units in one of its three blocks of the Peace Garden project in Shanghai had been sold and its 50 percent-owned Cimbria Court development had been sold to a third party on December 16, 1996, for HK$168 million, Hysan said.

Cheung said with the profit contribution from Hysan's Lee Gardens commercial development coming on stream in the second half of the year, and the booking from the Singapore project sale, the company should post better profit growth this year.

The completion of the Lee Gardens project was expected to be delayed to the second quarter of 1997. Hysan said more than 90 percent of the retail space and about 70 percent of the office space had been pre-leased to retailers, restaurants and companies.
"The pre-leasing of Lee Gardens looks good," said Cheung.
He forecast net profit growth of 18.5 percent in 1997 to HK$1.6 billion.
"The group's investment property portfolio would further be strengthened after the completion of the Lee Gardens and the acquisition of the Entertainment Building," Hysan said.
The HK$3.64 billion purchase of the Entertainment Building in Hong Kong's Central District is due to be completed on May 20.
Hysan said the Hong Kong property market is likely to remain active and rentals for luxury residential and commercial properties should rise in 1997.
Hysan shares fell to a day low of HK$24.35 after the results announcement before recovering slightly to close at HK$24.50, down HK$0.75 or nearly three percent from Tuesday.
Brokers said the selling pressure was limited and the fall was in line with the market. The Hang Seng Index tumbled 133.07 points, or one percent, to finish at 13,119.13.
"It's partly due to the weak sentiment in the property sector," said Raymond Ngai, senior investment analyst at UBS Securities.
He said Hysan shares should find support at HK$24.00, a 35 percent discount to the company's net asset value, which it put at HK$36.70 per share as of December 31, 1996.
